claim: 11 of the 26 transcripts that were increased in hans6 relative to wild-type were expressed in the pronephron at 20 hpf.
source: Surprisingly, 11 of the 26 transcripts that were increased in hans6 relative to wild-type were expressed in the pronephron, the embryonic kidney.
evidence: Based on microarray analysis comparing gene expression profiles at 20 hpf in wild-type and hans6 mutant embryos, as referenced in Garavito-Aguilar et al., 2010.

claim: The six genes with the most elevated expression in hans6 mutants are all expressed in the pronephron tubules.
source: The six genes with the most elevated expression in hans6 mutants (Garavito-Aguilar et al., 2010) are all expressed in the pronephron tubules.
evidence: Based on microarray data from Garavito-Aguilar et al., 2010.

claim: atp1a1a.4 expression is increased in tubule width in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: We examined the expression of two of these genes that are expressed throughout the tubules -- atp1a1a.4, which encodes a subunit of the Na+/K+ ATPase (Thisse et al., 2004), and cadherin17 (cdh17) (Horsfield et al., 2002) -- and observed an increase in tubule width in hans6 (Figure 1A–C, E–G).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A-C demonstrates widened expression of atp1a1a.4 in hans6 mutants compared to wild-type.

claim: cdh17 expression is increased in tubule width in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: We examined the expression of two of these genes that are expressed throughout the tubules -- atp1a1a.4, which encodes a subunit of the Na+/K+ ATPase (Thisse et al., 2004), and cadherin17 (cdh17) (Horsfield et al., 2002) -- and observed an increase in tubule width in hans6 (Figure 1A–C, E–G).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E-G demonstrates widened expression of cdh17 in hans6 mutants compared to wild-type.

claim: slc12a3 expression width is increased in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: A similar increase in width of expression was seen for another gene upregulated in hans6 but only expressed in a single tubule segment (Wingert et al., 2007), slc12a3 (Figure 1I–K), which encodes the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter solute carrier 12a3.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1I-K demonstrates widened expression of slc12a3 in hans6 mutants compared to wild-type.

claim: The anterior-posterior extent of slc12a3 expression is unaltered in hans6 mutants.
source: Notably, in contrast to its widened expression, the anterior-posterior extent of slc12a3 expression appeared unaltered.
evidence: Observation from in situ hybridization data comparing wild-type and hans6 mutants.

claim: Glomerular precursor populations are expanded in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: Last, by examining expression of lhx1a and pax2a, which mark glomerular precursors at 24 hpf (O'Brien et al., 2011), we found that the populations of glomerular precursors, like the tubules, were expanded in hans6 (Figure 1M–O and Figure 8B,C).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1M-O and Figure 8B-C demonstrates expanded expression of glomerular precursor markers in hans6 mutants.

claim: The number of cells in cross-section of the pronephron tubule is increased in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: We found that the number of cells seen in cross-section of the tubule was increased in hans6 (Figure 1Q–S).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 1Q-S demonstrates increased cell number per cross-section in hans6 mutants.

claim: The total tubule area in cross-section is increased in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: Concomitant with this increase in the number of cells, the total tubule area in cross-section was increased in hans6 mutants (Figure 1T).
evidence: Histological measurements shown in Figure 1T demonstrate increased tubule area in hans6 mutants with statistical significance (p<0.0001).

claim: Injection of hand2 mRNA inhibits pronephron formation at 24 hpf.
source: Injection of hand2 mRNA inhibited pronephron formation, as assessed by atp1a1a.4 expression (Figure 1D).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D demonstrates reduced atp1a1a.4 expression following hand2 mRNA injection.

claim: Heat shock-induced overexpression of hand2 results in pronephron defects comparable to those caused by mRNA injection.
source: Heat shock-induced overexpression resulted in pronephron defects comparable to those caused by mRNA injection, as assessed by atp1a1a.4, cdh17 and slc12a3 expression (Figure 1H,L and Figure 3A,B).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1H, L and Figure 3A, B demonstrates reduced pronephron marker expression following heat shock-induced hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression dramatically inhibits lhx1a expression in glomerular precursors at 24 hpf.
source: Furthermore, like tubule gene expression, lhx1a and pax2a expression in glomerular precursors was dramatically inhibited by hand2 overexpression (Figure 1P and data not shown), again emphasizing the broad effect of hand2 function on pronephron formation.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1P demonstrates reduced lhx1a expression in glomerular precursors following hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression does not affect atp1a1a.4 expression in mucus-secreting cells.
source: In contrast to these effects of hand2 overexpression on the pronephron, most other regions of expression of these markers, such as expression of atp1a1a.4 in mucus-secreting cells and expression of lhx1a in spinal neurons, were unaffected (Figure 1D,P).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D, P demonstrates that atp1a1a.4 expression in mucus-secreting cells and lhx1a expression in spinal neurons remain unaffected by hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression does not affect lhx1a expression in spinal neurons.
source: In contrast to these effects of hand2 overexpression on the pronephron, most other regions of expression of these markers, such as expression of atp1a1a.4 in mucus-secreting cells and expression of lhx1a in spinal neurons, were unaffected (Figure 1D,P).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1D, P demonstrates that lhx1a expression in spinal neurons remains unaffected by hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression causes a dramatic reduction in otic vesicle expression of atp1a1a.4.
source: Of note, however, we did observe a dramatic reduction in otic vesicle expression of both atp1a1a.4 and pax2a (data not shown), suggesting a shared susceptibility to hand2 overexpression in the otic vesicles and the pronephron.
evidence: Observation from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: hand2 overexpression causes a dramatic reduction in otic vesicle expression of pax2a.
source: Of note, however, we did observe a dramatic reduction in otic vesicle expression of both atp1a1a.4 and pax2a (data not shown), suggesting a shared susceptibility to hand2 overexpression in the otic vesicles and the pronephron.
evidence: Observation from in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: The width of the intermediate mesoderm is expanded in hans6 mutants at the 6, 10 and 12 somite stages.
source: Indeed, using two established IM markers, pax2a and lhx1a, we observed that the width of the IM was expanded in hans6 mutants and hand2 morphants (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), at stages shortly after gastrulation (i.e. at the 6, 10 and 12 somite stages).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B demonstrates widened IM marker expression in hans6 mutants.

claim: The width of the intermediate mesoderm is expanded in hand2 morphants at the 6, 10 and 12 somite stages.
source: Indeed, using two established IM markers, pax2a and lhx1a, we observed that the width of the IM was expanded in hans6 mutants and hand2 morphants (Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B), at stages shortly after gastrulation (i.e. at the 6, 10 and 12 somite stages).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B demonstrates widened IM marker expression in hand2 morphants.

claim: There is no substantial difference in the length of the intermediate mesoderm between wild-type and hans6 mutant embryos.
source: In contrast, there was no substantial difference in the length of the IM seen in wild-type and hans6 mutant embryos (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A, B demonstrates comparable anterior-posterior extent of IM in wild-type and hans6 mutants.

claim: hans6 mutants have approximately 50% more Pax2a+ IM cells than wild-type embryos at the 12 somite stage.
source: Furthermore, compared to wild-type embryos, hans6 mutants typically had ~50% more Pax2a+ IM cells (Figure 2D,E,G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2D, E, G demonstrates approximately 50% increase in Pax2a+ cells in hans6 mutants.

claim: The accumulation of IM cells in hans6 mutants does not appear to be associated with heightened proliferation within the IM.
source: This accumulation of IM cells did not appear to be associated with heightened proliferation within the IM (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Proliferation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 demonstrates no significant difference in proliferation index between wild-type and hans6 mutants.

claim: hand2 overexpression results in loss of intermediate mesoderm at the 11 somite stage.
source: Both hand2 mRNA injection and heat shock-induced overexpression of hand2 resulted in loss of IM, as determined by pax2a and lhx1a expression (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C demonstrates loss of IM marker expression following hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2-overexpressing embryos exhibit phenotypes ranging from a significantly reduced number of Pax2a+ IM cells to a complete absence of Pax2a+ IM at the 12 somite stage.
source: More specifically, hand2-overexpressing embryos exhibited phenotypes ranging from a significantly reduced number of Pax2a+ IM cells to a complete absence of Pax2a+ IM (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2F, G demonstrates reduced or absent Pax2a+ cells following hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression at the tailbud stage results in loss of the majority of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: For example, while inhibition at the tailbud or 2 somite stages resulted in the loss of the majority of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression (Figure 3A,B), inhibition at the 6 somite stage resulted in only a mild reduction (Figure 3D).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A demonstrates loss of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression following heat shock at tailbud stage.

claim: hand2 overexpression at the 2 somite stage results in loss of the majority of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: For example, while inhibition at the tailbud or 2 somite stages resulted in the loss of the majority of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression (Figure 3A,B), inhibition at the 6 somite stage resulted in only a mild reduction (Figure 3D).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B demonstrates loss of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression following heat shock at 2 somite stage.

claim: hand2 overexpression at the 6 somite stage results in only a mild reduction of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: For example, while inhibition at the tailbud or 2 somite stages resulted in the loss of the majority of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression (Figure 3A,B), inhibition at the 6 somite stage resulted in only a mild reduction (Figure 3D).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3D demonstrates mild reduction of pronephric atp1a1a.4 expression following heat shock at 6 somite stage.

claim: hand2 overexpression at the 10 somite stage does not disrupt pronephron development at 24 hpf.
source: Unlike overexpression at the tailbud, 2 somite, or 6 somite stages (Figure 3A–D), overexpression at the 10 somite stage failed to inhibit pronephron development (Figure 3E).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3E demonstrates unaffected pronephron development following heat shock at 10 somite stage.

claim: There is a hand2-sensitive phase of IM specification prior to the 10 somite stage.
source: Overall, our analysis suggests that there is a hand2-sensitive phase of IM specification prior to the 10 somite stage.
evidence: Based on temporal analysis of hand2 overexpression effects shown in Figure 3, demonstrating that overexpression before 10 somites affects IM but not after.

claim: hand2 is expressed in bilateral regions immediately lateral to the intermediate mesoderm during the hand2-sensitive phase of IM formation.
source: During the hand2-sensitive phase of IM formation, we found hand2 to be expressed in bilateral regions immediately lateral to the IM (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Fluorescent in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A, B demonstrates hand2 expression lateral to IM markers.

claim: hand2 is expressed lateral to multiple markers of blood and vessel progenitors, including etv2, tal1, and gata1.
source: At these stages, hand2 was also expressed lateral to multiple markers of blood and vessel progenitors, including etv2, tal1, and gata1 (Figure 4C and data not shown).
evidence: Fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C demonstrates hand2 expression lateral to vessel/blood progenitor markers.

claim: A gap lies between blood and vessel progenitor markers and the hand2-expressing cells.
source: However, a gap lies between these markers and the hand2-expressing cells, consistent with the IM residing between the lateral hand2-expressing cells and the medial blood and vessel progenitors (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C, D demonstrates spatial separation between hand2 expression and vessel/blood progenitor markers.

claim: A second, lateral population of vessel progenitors arises at the interface between the IM and the hand2-expressing cells at approximately the 11 somite stage.
source: We also found that the relationship between hand2 expression, the IM, and blood and vessel progenitors changed after the completion of the hand2-sensitive phase of IM formation. At approximately the 11 somite stage, a second, lateral population of vessel progenitors arises at the interface between the IM and the hand2-expressing cells (Figure 4F–I).
evidence: Fluorescent in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F-I demonstrates appearance of lateral vessel progenitors at the interface between hand2-expressing cells and IM.

claim: The lateral vessel progenitors are likely to be venous progenitors.
source: These lateral vessel progenitors are likely to be venous progenitors, based on the results of a prior study that suggested that the medial, earlier-forming vessel progenitors contribute to the dorsal aorta and that the lateral, later-forming vessel progenitors contribute to the primary cardinal vein (Kohli et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on prior lineage tracing study by Kohli et al., 2013.

claim: Expression of etv2 and tal1 in the medial population of vessel and blood progenitors is unaffected in hans6 mutants at the 6 and 10 somite stages.
source: To address this possibility, we first assessed the early expression of etv2, tal1, and gata1 in the medial population of vessel and blood progenitors, and we observed no differences between wild-type and hans6 mutant embryos at either the 6 or 10 somite stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and data not shown).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 demonstrates unaffected medial vessel/blood progenitor marker expression in hans6 mutants at early stages.

claim: Expression of etv2 in the lateral venous progenitor population is absent in hans6 mutants after the 11 somite stage.
source: In contrast, after the 11 somite stage, expression of both etv2 and tal1 in the lateral venous progenitor population was absent in hans6 mutants (Figure 5A,B,F,G).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A, B demonstrates absence of lateral etv2 expression in hans6 mutants at 12 somite stage.

claim: Expression of tal1 in the lateral venous progenitor population is absent in hans6 mutants after the 11 somite stage.
source: In contrast, after the 11 somite stage, expression of both etv2 and tal1 in the lateral venous progenitor population was absent in hans6 mutants (Figure 5A,B,F,G).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5F, G demonstrates absence of lateral tal1 expression in hans6 mutants at 12 somite stage.

claim: The formation of the lateral venous progenitors requires hand2.
source: Thus, the formation of the lateral venous progenitors, the appearance of which coincides with the end of the hand2-responsive phase of IM formation, requires hand2.
evidence: Based on loss of lateral venous progenitor markers in hans6 mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Overexpression of hand2 results in an expansion of etv2 expression in the posterior mesoderm at the 12 somite stage.
source: Overexpression of hand2 resulted in an expansion of both etv2 and tal1 expression in the posterior mesoderm (Figure 5C,H).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C demonstrates expanded etv2 expression following hand2 overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of hand2 results in an expansion of tal1 expression in the posterior mesoderm at the 12 somite stage.
source: Overexpression of hand2 resulted in an expansion of both etv2 and tal1 expression in the posterior mesoderm (Figure 5C,H).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5H demonstrates expanded tal1 expression following hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression results in a reduction of gata1 expression at the 12 somite stage.
source: In contrast, hand2 overexpression resulted in a reduction of gata1 expression (Figure 5M).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5M demonstrates reduced gata1 expression following hand2 overexpression.

claim: hans6 mutants lack mrc1a expression in the posterior cardinal vein at 24 hpf.
source: Similarly, hans6 mutants lack mrc1a and flt4 expression in the posterior cardinal vein, suggesting a defect in venous development (Figure 6A,B,D,E).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A, B demonstrates absence of mrc1a expression in the posterior cardinal vein in hans6 mutants.

claim: hans6 mutants lack flt4 expression in the posterior cardinal vein at the 20 somite stage.
source: Similarly, hans6 mutants lack mrc1a and flt4 expression in the posterior cardinal vein, suggesting a defect in venous development (Figure 6A,B,D,E).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6D, E demonstrates absence of flt4 expression in the posterior cardinal vein in hans6 mutants.

claim: The posterior cardinal vein is present in hans6 mutants at 28 hpf.
source: Using Tg(flk1:ras-mcherry) to label the entire vasculature, we identified the presence of the posterior cardinal vein in hans6 mutants (Figure 6J–L), but found that their caudal venous plexus failed to be properly remodeled (Figure 6M–O).
evidence: Confocal imaging of Tg(flk1:ras-mcherry) shown in Figure 6J-L demonstrates presence of posterior cardinal vein in hans6 mutants.

claim: The caudal venous plexus fails to be properly remodeled in hans6 mutants at 32 hpf.
source: Using Tg(flk1:ras-mcherry) to label the entire vasculature, we identified the presence of the posterior cardinal vein in hans6 mutants (Figure 6J–L), but found that their caudal venous plexus failed to be properly remodeled (Figure 6M–O).
evidence: Confocal imaging of Tg(flk1:ras-mcherry) shown in Figure 6M-O demonstrates defective remodeling of caudal venous plexus in hans6 mutants.

claim: flt4 expression in the dorsal aorta is grossly unaffected in hans6 mutants at the 20 somite stage.
source: In contrast to these changes in the venous system, flt4 and ephrin-b2a (efnb2a) expression in the dorsal aorta, as well as mrc1a expression in the posterior blood island, appeared grossly unaffected by hand2 loss-of-function (Figure 6B,E,H).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6E demonstrates unaffected flt4 expression in the dorsal aorta in hans6 mutants.

claim: efnb2a expression in the dorsal aorta is grossly unaffected in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: In contrast to these changes in the venous system, flt4 and ephrin-b2a (efnb2a) expression in the dorsal aorta, as well as mrc1a expression in the posterior blood island, appeared grossly unaffected by hand2 loss-of-function (Figure 6B,E,H).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6H demonstrates unaffected efnb2a expression in the dorsal aorta in hans6 mutants.

claim: mrc1a expression in the posterior blood island is grossly unaffected in hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: In contrast to these changes in the venous system, flt4 and ephrin-b2a (efnb2a) expression in the dorsal aorta, as well as mrc1a expression in the posterior blood island, appeared grossly unaffected by hand2 loss-of-function (Figure 6B,E,H).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6B demonstrates unaffected mrc1a expression in the posterior blood island in hans6 mutants.

claim: hand2 overexpression increases vascular expression of mrc1a at 24 hpf.
source: Meanwhile, consistent with the ability of hand2 to promote vessel progenitor formation, hand2 overexpression increased vascular expression of mrc1a, flt4, and efnb2a (Figure 6C,F,I).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6C demonstrates increased mrc1a expression following hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression increases vascular expression of flt4 at the 20 somite stage.
source: Meanwhile, consistent with the ability of hand2 to promote vessel progenitor formation, hand2 overexpression increased vascular expression of mrc1a, flt4, and efnb2a (Figure 6C,F,I).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6F demonstrates increased flt4 expression following hand2 overexpression.

claim: hand2 overexpression increases vascular expression of efnb2a at 24 hpf.
source: Meanwhile, consistent with the ability of hand2 to promote vessel progenitor formation, hand2 overexpression increased vascular expression of mrc1a, flt4, and efnb2a (Figure 6C,F,I).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6I demonstrates increased efnb2a expression following hand2 overexpression.

claim: The dimensions of the hand2 expression territory are comparable in wild-type and hand2 morphant embryos at the 10 somite stage.
source: Importantly, however, we observed comparable dimensions of the hand2 expression territory in wild-type and morphant embryos (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7A, B demonstrates comparable extent of hand2 expression territory in wild-type and hand2 morphants.

claim: There is no significant difference between the numbers of GFP+ cells in the posterior mesoderm of wild-type and hans6 mutant embryos carrying Tg(hand2:EGFP) at the 12 somite stage.
source: More specifically, when using Tg(hand2:EGFP), we found no significant difference between the numbers of GFP+ cells in the posterior mesoderm of wild-type and hans6 mutant embryos (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 7C-E demonstrates no significant difference in GFP+ cell numbers between wild-type and hans6 mutants.

claim: Approximately 6% of the GFP+ cells in the posterior mesoderm of wild-type embryos carrying Tg(hand2:EGFP) also display Pax2a at the 12 somite stage.
source: Careful examination of wild-type embryos carrying the Tg(hand2:EGFP) transgene revealed that ~6% of the GFP+ cells in their posterior mesoderm also displayed the IM marker Pax2a (Figure 7C,E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 7C, E demonstrates approximately 6% of GFP+ cells are also Pax2a+ in wild-type embryos.

claim: Approximately 60% of the GFP+ cells in the posterior mesoderm of hans6 mutant embryos carrying Tg(hand2:EGFP) are also Pax2a+ at the 12 somite stage.
source: In dramatic contrast, ~60% of the GFP+ cells in the hans6 mutant posterior mesoderm were also Pax2a+ (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 7D, E demonstrates approximately 60% of GFP+ cells are also Pax2a+ in hans6 mutants.

claim: The GFP+ Pax2a+ cells are typically observed at or near the border where the hand2-expressing cells meet the IM in embryos carrying Tg(hand2:EGFP).
source: Intriguingly, the GFP+ Pax2a+ cells were typically observed at or near the border where the hand2-expressing cells meet the IM (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C, D demonstrates spatial localization of GFP+ Pax2a+ cells at the border between hand2-expressing cells and IM.

claim: hand2 and osr1 are co-expressed in the lateral posterior mesoderm at the 6 somite stage.
source: Through direct comparison of hand2 and osr1 expression patterns, we found that the genes are co-expressed in the lateral posterior mesoderm (Figure 8A).
evidence: Fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8A demonstrates overlapping expression of hand2 and osr1.

claim: osr1 morphants exhibit inhibited pronephron development.
source: Additionally, prior studies demonstrated that loss of osr1 function results in phenotypes opposite to those caused by loss of hand2: in contrast to the expanded pronephron and defective venous vasculature in hans6 mutants, osr1 morphants were found to exhibit inhibited pronephron development together with expansion of venous structures (Mudumana et al., 2008; Tena et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Mudumana et al., 2008 and Tena et al., 2007.

claim: osr1 morphants exhibit expansion of venous structures.
source: Additionally, prior studies demonstrated that loss of osr1 function results in phenotypes opposite to those caused by loss of hand2: in contrast to the expanded pronephron and defective venous vasculature in hans6 mutants, osr1 morphants were found to exhibit inhibited pronephron development together with expansion of venous structures (Mudumana et al., 2008; Tena et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Mudumana et al., 2008 and Tena et al., 2007.

claim: pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors is expanded in 100% of hans6 mutants at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (B), pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors (arrow) was expanded in 100% of hans6 mutants (C, n=11), absent (48%) or reduced (48%) in osr1 morphants (D, n=25), and relatively normal in hans6 + osr1 MO embryos (E, n=11).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8B, C demonstrates expanded pax2a expression in glomerular and neck precursors in hans6 mutants.

claim: pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors is absent in 48% of osr1 morphants at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (B), pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors (arrow) was expanded in 100% of hans6 mutants (C, n=11), absent (48%) or reduced (48%) in osr1 morphants (D, n=25), and relatively normal in hans6 + osr1 MO embryos (E, n=11).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8D demonstrates absent pax2a expression in glomerular and neck precursors in 48% of osr1 morphants.

claim: pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors is reduced in 48% of osr1 morphants at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (B), pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors (arrow) was expanded in 100% of hans6 mutants (C, n=11), absent (48%) or reduced (48%) in osr1 morphants (D, n=25), and relatively normal in hans6 + osr1 MO embryos (E, n=11).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8D demonstrates reduced pax2a expression in glomerular and neck precursors in 48% of osr1 morphants.

claim: pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors is relatively normal in hans6 mutants injected with osr1 morpholino at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (B), pax2a expression in the glomerular and neck precursors (arrow) was expanded in 100% of hans6 mutants (C, n=11), absent (48%) or reduced (48%) in osr1 morphants (D, n=25), and relatively normal in hans6 + osr1 MO embryos (E, n=11).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8E demonstrates relatively normal pax2a expression in glomerular and neck precursors in hans6 + osr1 MO embryos.

claim: 85% of hans6 mutants have wide pronephric tubules as assessed by atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (F), atp1a1a.4 expression in the pronephric tubules was wide in 85% of hans6 mutants (G, n=13), while many osr1 morphants (H, n=133) had tubules with shortened anterior expression (18%) or tubules with segmental losses (35%), and 47% of osr1 morphants had a wild-type appearance.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8F, G demonstrates wide atp1a1a.4 expression in pronephric tubules in 85% of hans6 mutants.

claim: 18% of osr1 morphants have pronephric tubules with shortened anterior atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (F), atp1a1a.4 expression in the pronephric tubules was wide in 85% of hans6 mutants (G, n=13), while many osr1 morphants (H, n=133) had tubules with shortened anterior expression (18%) or tubules with segmental losses (35%), and 47% of osr1 morphants had a wild-type appearance.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8H demonstrates shortened anterior atp1a1a.4 expression in pronephric tubules in 18% of osr1 morphants.

claim: 35% of osr1 morphants have pronephric tubules with segmental losses of atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (F), atp1a1a.4 expression in the pronephric tubules was wide in 85% of hans6 mutants (G, n=13), while many osr1 morphants (H, n=133) had tubules with shortened anterior expression (18%) or tubules with segmental losses (35%), and 47% of osr1 morphants had a wild-type appearance.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8H demonstrates segmental losses of atp1a1a.4 expression in pronephric tubules in 35% of osr1 morphants.

claim: 47% of osr1 morphants have wild-type appearance of pronephric tubules as assessed by atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: Compared to wild-type (F), atp1a1a.4 expression in the pronephric tubules was wide in 85% of hans6 mutants (G, n=13), while many osr1 morphants (H, n=133) had tubules with shortened anterior expression (18%) or tubules with segmental losses (35%), and 47% of osr1 morphants had a wild-type appearance.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8H demonstrates wild-type appearance of atp1a1a.4 expression in pronephric tubules in 47% of osr1 morphants.

claim: 85% of hans6 mutants injected with osr1 morpholino have wild-type appearance of pronephric tubules as assessed by atp1a1a.4 expression at 24 hpf.
source: 85% of hans6 + osr1 MO embryos (I, n=46) resembled wild-type, whereas 11% had a shortened anterior tubule and 4% had segmental losses in the tubules.
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8I demonstrates wild-type appearance of atp1a1a.4 expression in pronephric tubules in 85% of hans6 + osr1 MO embryos.

claim: Loss of hand2 function does not affect the intensity or dimensions of osr1 expression.
source: We found, however, that loss of hand2 function did not seem to affect the intensity or dimensions of osr1 expression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B demonstrates unaffected osr1 expression in hans6 mutants.

claim: osr1 loss-of-function does not alter hand2 expression.
source: Similarly, osr1 loss-of-function did not appear to alter hand2 expression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: In situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D demonstrates unaffected hand2 expression in osr1 morphants.

claim: hand2 and osr1 function in parallel genetic pathways that act in opposition to regulate the precise dimensions of the pronephron.
source: Therefore, hand2 and osr1 appear to affect downstream gene expression independently, without affecting one another's expression. Furthermore, our data suggest that hand2 and osr1 function in parallel genetic pathways that act in opposition in order to regulate the precise dimensions of the pronephron.
evidence: Based on genetic interaction data showing that double loss-of-function largely restores normal pronephron development, and expression analysis showing no mutual regulation.

claim: Hand2 is expressed in the posterior mesoderm of zebrafish embryos.
source: Prior studies had demonstrated bilateral hand2 expression in the posterior mesoderm of zebrafish, mouse, chick, and Xenopus embryos (Angelo et al., 2000; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2000; Srivastava et al., 1997; Thomas et al., 1998; Yelon et al., 2000; Yin et al., 2010), but the precise localization of this expression relative to the IM had not been determined.
evidence: Based on prior studies including Yelon et al., 2000.

claim: Hand2 is expressed in the posterior mesoderm of mouse embryos.
source: Prior studies had demonstrated bilateral hand2 expression in the posterior mesoderm of zebrafish, mouse, chick, and Xenopus embryos (Angelo et al., 2000; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2000; Srivastava et al., 1997; Thomas et al., 1998; Yelon et al., 2000; Yin et al., 2010), but the precise localization of this expression relative to the IM had not been determined.
evidence: Based on prior studies including Srivastava et al., 1997 and Thomas et al., 1998.

claim: Hand2 is expressed in the posterior mesoderm of chick embryos.
source: Prior studies had demonstrated bilateral hand2 expression in the posterior mesoderm of zebrafish, mouse, chick, and Xenopus embryos (Angelo et al., 2000; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2000; Srivastava et al., 1997; Thomas et al., 1998; Yelon et al., 2000; Yin et al., 2010), but the precise localization of this expression relative to the IM had not been determined.
evidence: Based on prior studies including Angelo et al., 2000 and Fernandez-Teran et al., 2000.

claim: Hand2 is expressed in the posterior mesoderm of Xenopus embryos.
source: Prior studies had demonstrated bilateral hand2 expression in the posterior mesoderm of zebrafish, mouse, chick, and Xenopus embryos (Angelo et al., 2000; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2000; Srivastava et al., 1997; Thomas et al., 1998; Yelon et al., 2000; Yin et al., 2010), but the precise localization of this expression relative to the IM had not been determined.
evidence: Based on prior studies including Yin et al., 2010.

claim: Kidney progenitor cells originate from the intermediate mesoderm.
source: Kidney progenitor cells originate from the intermediate mesoderm (IM), a pair of narrow bilateral stripes within the posterior mesoderm, flanked by lateral mesoderm that gives rise to vessels and blood and by paraxial mesoderm that gives rise to bone, cartilage, and skeletal muscle.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field of developmental biology.

claim: The intermediate mesoderm is flanked by lateral mesoderm that gives rise to vessels and blood.
source: Kidney progenitor cells originate from the intermediate mesoderm (IM), a pair of narrow bilateral stripes within the posterior mesoderm, flanked by lateral mesoderm that gives rise to vessels and blood and by paraxial mesoderm that gives rise to bone, cartilage, and skeletal muscle.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field of developmental biology.

claim: The intermediate mesoderm is flanked by paraxial mesoderm that gives rise to bone, cartilage, and skeletal muscle.
source: Kidney progenitor cells originate from the intermediate mesoderm (IM), a pair of narrow bilateral stripes within the posterior mesoderm, flanked by lateral mesoderm that gives rise to vessels and blood and by paraxial mesoderm that gives rise to bone, cartilage, and skeletal muscle.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field of developmental biology.

claim: Lhx1/Lim1 is expressed in the intermediate mesoderm and is required for its development.
source: Several conserved transcription factors are expressed in the IM and are required for its development, including Lhx1/Lim1, Pax2, and Osr1/Odd1 (Dressler and Douglass, 1992; James et al., 2006; Krauss et al., 1991; Toyama and Dawid, 1997; Tsang et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on prior studies including Krauss et al., 1991 and Toyama and Dawid, 1997.

claim: Pax2 is expressed in the intermediate mesoderm and is required for its development.
source: Several conserved transcription factors are expressed in the IM and are required for its development, including Lhx1/Lim1, Pax2, and Osr1/Odd1 (Dressler and Douglass, 1992; James et al., 2006; Krauss et al., 1991; Toyama and Dawid, 1997; Tsang et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on prior studies including Dressler and Douglass, 1992.

claim: Osr1/Odd1 is expressed in the intermediate mesoderm and is required for its development.
source: Several conserved transcription factors are expressed in the IM and are required for its development, including Lhx1/Lim1, Pax2, and Osr1/Odd1 (Dressler and Douglass, 1992; James et al., 2006; Krauss et al., 1991; Toyama and Dawid, 1997; Tsang et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on prior studies including Tsang et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2005; and James et al., 2006.

claim: Low levels of BMP signaling promote intermediate mesoderm formation.
source: Furthermore, TGF-beta signaling acts in a dose-dependent manner to pattern the medial-lateral axis of the posterior mesoderm: for example, low levels of BMP signaling promote IM formation while high levels of BMP signaling promote lateral mesoderm formation (Fleming et al., 2013; James and Schultheiss, 2005).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Fleming et al., 2013 and James and Schultheiss, 2005.

claim: High levels of BMP signaling promote lateral mesoderm formation.
source: Furthermore, TGF-beta signaling acts in a dose-dependent manner to pattern the medial-lateral axis of the posterior mesoderm: for example, low levels of BMP signaling promote IM formation while high levels of BMP signaling promote lateral mesoderm formation (Fleming et al., 2013; James and Schultheiss, 2005).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Fleming et al., 2013 and James and Schultheiss, 2005.

claim: In chick, mouse, and Xenopus, Osr1 and Lim1 are expressed in both the lateral mesoderm and the IM before becoming restricted to the IM.
source: In chick, mouse, and Xenopus, Osr1 and Lim1 are expressed in both the lateral mesoderm and the IM before becoming restricted to the IM, implying the existence of a mechanism that acts to exclude IM gene expression from the neighboring lateral territory (Carroll and Vize, 1999; James et al., 2006; Mugford et al., 2008; Tsang et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on prior studies including Carroll and Vize, 1999; James et al., 2006; Mugford et al., 2008; and Tsang et al., 2000.

claim: Overexpression of tal1 and lmo2 induces ectopic vessel and blood specification while inhibiting IM formation.
source: Additional data have hinted at an antagonistic relationship between the IM and the blood and vessel lineages (Gering et al., 2003; Gupta et al., 2006): for example, overexpression of vascular and hematopoietic transcription factors (tal1 and lmo2) induces ectopic vessel and blood specification while inhibiting IM formation (Gering et al., 2003).
evidence: Based on prior study by Gering et al., 2003.

claim: Zebrafish osr1 morphants exhibit disrupted pronephron formation together with expanded venous structures.
source: Along the same lines, zebrafish osr1 morphants exhibit disrupted pronephron formation together with expanded venous structures (Mudumana et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on prior study by Mudumana et al., 2008.

claim: Hand2 has functions in the heart, limb, and branchial arches.
source: Prior studies of Hand2 have focused on its functions in other tissues, including the heart, limb, and branchial arches (e.g. Charité et al., 2000; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2000; Funato et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2003; Srivastava et al., 1997; Yanagisawa et al., 2003; Yelon et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on prior studies including Charité et al., 2000; Fernandez-Teran et al., 2000; Funato et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2003; Srivastava et al., 1997; Yanagisawa et al., 2003; and Yelon et al., 2000.

claim: hand2 limits the size of the embryonic kidney by restricting intermediate mesoderm dimensions.
source: Here, we show that the bHLH transcription factor Hand2 limits the size of the embryonic kidney by restricting IM dimensions.
evidence: Based on loss-of-function and gain-of-function studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: hand2 promotes venous development while inhibiting IM formation at the interface between hand2-expressing cells and the IM.
source: Venous progenitors arise between these two territories, and hand2 promotes venous development while inhibiting IM formation at this interface.
evidence: Based on expression analysis and loss-of-function studies showing loss of lateral venous progenitors and expansion of IM in hand2 mutants.

claim: hand2 and osr1 have functionally antagonistic influences on kidney development.
source: Furthermore, hand2 and the co-expressed zinc-finger transcription factor osr1 have functionally antagonistic influences on kidney development.
evidence: Based on genetic interaction studies showing that double loss-of-function largely restores normal pronephron development.

claim: hand2 functions in opposition to osr1 to balance the formation of kidney and vein progenitors by regulating cell fate decisions at the lateral boundary of the IM.
source: Together, our data suggest that hand2 functions in opposition to osr1 to balance the formation of kidney and vein progenitors by regulating cell fate decisions at the lateral boundary of the IM.
evidence: Based on combined analysis of expression patterns, loss-of-function phenotypes, and genetic interactions.

claim: Intensity of hand2 expression appears higher in hand2 loss-of-function embryos.
source: Of note, each of these approaches indicated heightened intensity of hand2 expression in hand2 loss-of-function embryos (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting the possibility that hand2 acts to inhibit its own expression.
evidence: In situ hybridization and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A, B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 demonstrates higher intensity of hand2 expression in hand2 loss-of-function embryos.

claim: hand2 may act to inhibit its own expression.
source: Of note, each of these approaches indicated heightened intensity of hand2 expression in hand2 loss-of-function embryos (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting the possibility that hand2 acts to inhibit its own expression.
evidence: Based on observation of heightened hand2 expression in hand2 loss-of-function embryos.

claim: The expansion of the IM in hans6 mutants does not come at the expense of the formation of cells that normally express hand2.
source: Thus, it seems that the expansion of the IM in hans6 mutants does not come at the expense of the formation of cells that normally express hand2.
evidence: Based on quantification showing no significant difference in GFP+ cell numbers between wild-type and hans6 mutants carrying Tg(hand2:EGFP).

claim: hand2 limits IM dimensions by constraining the lateral boundary of the IM through repression of IM gene expression within hand2-expressing cells.
source: These data suggest that hand2 limits IM dimensions by constraining the lateral boundary of the IM through repression of IM gene expression within hand2-expressing cells.
evidence: Based on observation that ~60% of GFP+ cells in hans6 mutants are also Pax2a+, compared to ~6% in wild-type.

claim: Inhibition of etv2 function at the time when lateral vessel progenitors arise results in loss of mrc1a expression in the cardinal vein.
source: Furthermore, this study found that inhibition of etv2 function at the time when these lateral cells arise results in loss of expression of mannose receptor c1a (mrc1a), a marker of the cardinal vein (Kohli et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on prior study by Kohli et al., 2013.

claim: There are case reports of chromosomal duplications containing HAND2 in patients with renal hypoplasia.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that there are case reports of chromosomal duplications containing HAND2 in patients with renal hypoplasia (Otsuka et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on prior case report by Otsuka et al., 2005.

claim: The endoderm is expanded in osr1 morphants.
source: The endoderm is expanded in osr1 morphants, and mutations that disrupt endoderm development abrogate the pronephron defects caused by osr1 loss-of-function (Mudumana et al., 2008; Terashima et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Mudumana et al., 2008 and Terashima et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations that disrupt endoderm development abrogate the pronephron defects caused by osr1 loss-of-function.
source: The endoderm is expanded in osr1 morphants, and mutations that disrupt endoderm development abrogate the pronephron defects caused by osr1 loss-of-function (Mudumana et al., 2008; Terashima et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Mudumana et al., 2008 and Terashima et al., 2014.

claim: hans6 mutants exhibit normal amounts of endoderm.
source: We observe ectopic Pax2a+ cells emerging within hand2-expressing mesoderm in hand2 mutants; additionally, whereas osr1 morphants have an expansion of the endoderm (Mudumana et al., 2008; Terashima et al., 2014), hans6 mutants exhibit normal amounts of endoderm (Wendl et al., 2007; Yelon et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Wendl et al., 2007 and Yelon et al., 2000.

claim: Osr1 has a role in IM and kidney development in mouse, chick, and Xenopus.
source: Loss-of-function and gain-of-function studies in mouse, chick, and Xenopus have demonstrated a role for Osr1 in IM and kidney development through focused analyses of histology and gene expression patterns (James et al., 2006; Mugford et al., 2008; Tena et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on prior studies including James et al., 2006; Mugford et al., 2008; Tena et al., 2007; and Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Hand2 and Hand1 are both expressed in the murine lateral posterior mesoderm.
source: Moreover, future investigations in mouse may need to evaluate potential redundancy between the functions of Hand2 and Hand1: both of these genes are expressed in the murine lateral posterior mesoderm (Thomas et al., 1998), whereas zebrafish have only a single Hand gene.
evidence: Based on prior study by Thomas et al., 1998.

claim: Zebrafish have only a single Hand gene.
source: Moreover, future investigations in mouse may need to evaluate potential redundancy between the functions of Hand2 and Hand1: both of these genes are expressed in the murine lateral posterior mesoderm (Thomas et al., 1998), whereas zebrafish have only a single Hand gene.
evidence: Established knowledge about zebrafish genetics.

claim: Disease-causing mutations in PAX2 have been identified in some cases of CAKUT.
source: In some cases of CAKUT, disease-causing mutations have been identified, many of which disrupt genes that influence early kidney development, including mutations in PAX2 and OSR1 (Madariaga et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on prior studies including Madariaga et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2011; and Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: Disease-causing mutations in OSR1 have been identified in some cases of CAKUT.
source: In some cases of CAKUT, disease-causing mutations have been identified, many of which disrupt genes that influence early kidney development, including mutations in PAX2 and OSR1 (Madariaga et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on prior studies including Madariaga et al., 2013; Thomas et al., 2011; and Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: hand2 is necessary to constrain the size of the pronephron.
source: Taken together, our loss-of-function and gain-of-function studies show that hand2 is necessary to constrain the size of the pronephron, likely through an ability to repress pronephron formation.
evidence: Based on loss-of-function studies showing expanded pronephron and gain-of-function studies showing reduced pronephron.

claim: hand2 likely constrains the size of the pronephron through an ability to repress pronephron formation.
source: Taken together, our loss-of-function and gain-of-function studies show that hand2 is necessary to constrain the size of the pronephron, likely through an ability to repress pronephron formation.
evidence: Based on gain-of-function studies showing that hand2 overexpression can inhibit pronephron formation.

claim: hand2 restricts the initial formation of the IM.
source: Thus, our data suggest that hand2 restricts the initial formation of the IM.
evidence: Based on observation of expanded IM in hans6 mutants at early stages (6, 10, 12 somites) and increased Pax2a+ cell numbers without increased proliferation.

claim: hand2 limits the dimensions of the IM by repressing its initial specification.
source: Taken together with our loss-of-function analyses, these results suggest that hand2 limits the dimensions of the IM by repressing its initial specification.
evidence: Based on combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function studies showing expanded IM in mutants and reduced/absent IM with overexpression.

claim: hand2 is required for the successful execution of certain aspects of venous differentiation, including the expression of characteristic venous markers.
source: Overall, these studies demonstrate a previously unappreciated role for hand2 in regulating trunk vasculature development. More specifically, our data indicate that hand2 is required for the successful execution of certain aspects of venous differentiation, including the expression of characteristic venous markers and the remodeling of the caudal venous plexus.
evidence: Based on loss of mrc1a and flt4 expression in the posterior cardinal vein in hans6 mutants.

claim: hand2 is required for the successful execution of certain aspects of venous differentiation, including the remodeling of the caudal venous plexus.
source: Overall, these studies demonstrate a previously unappreciated role for hand2 in regulating trunk vasculature development. More specifically, our data indicate that hand2 is required for the successful execution of certain aspects of venous differentiation, including the expression of characteristic venous markers and the remodeling of the caudal venous plexus.
evidence: Based on defective remodeling of the caudal venous plexus in hans6 mutants.

claim: hand2 implements its functions in venous differentiation by promoting the development of the lateral venous progenitors.
source: Combined with prior lineage tracing studies and etv2 loss-of-function analysis (Kohli et al., 2013), our findings suggest that hand2 implements these functions by promoting the development of the lateral venous progenitors.
evidence: Based on loss of lateral venous progenitor markers in hand2 mutants and prior lineage tracing studies by Kohli et al., 2013.

claim: The roles of hand2 in venous progenitor formation and venous differentiation may be independent of one another.
source: We cannot, however, rule out the possibility that the roles of hand2 in venous progenitor formation and venous differentiation are independent of one another, such that the differentiation defects represent a later influence of hand2 on vascular development.
evidence: Speculation about alternative interpretation of the data.

claim: Hand2 could act cell-autonomously to inhibit IM specification.
source: Perhaps hand2 acts cell-autonomously to inhibit IM specification; the ectopic appearance of Pax2a+ cells within the hand2-expressing territory in hand2 mutants makes this an attractive model.
evidence: Speculation based on observation of ectopic Pax2a+ cells within hand2-expressing territory in hand2 mutants.

claim: Hand2 could have a non-autonomous influence on IM dimensions by regulating the production of a lateralizing signal.
source: Alternatively, hand2 could have a non-autonomous influence on IM dimensions, perhaps by regulating the production of a lateralizing signal, the absence of which would result in the lateral expansion of IM gene expression.
evidence: Speculation about alternative mechanism of hand2 function.

claim: The role of hand2 could interface with the BMP signaling pathway.
source: In this scenario, it is tempting to speculate that the role of hand2 could interface with the BMP signaling pathway, considering its prior implication in posterior mesoderm patterning (James and Schultheiss, 2005).
evidence: Speculation based on prior implication of BMP signaling in posterior mesoderm patterning by James and Schultheiss, 2005.

claim: hand2 prevents lateral hand2+osr1+ cells from acquiring more medial characteristics, such as expression of pax2a or lhx1a.
source: Wherever its precise location of action may be, this function of hand2 -- preventing lateral hand2+osr1+ cells from acquiring more medial characteristics, such as expression of pax2a or lhx1a --suggests a possible mechanism for distinguishing IM gene expression from that of neighboring lateral territories, a distinct process required during both in vivo (James et al., 2006) and in vitro (Takasato et al., 2014) IM development.
evidence: Based on observation of ectopic pax2a expression in hand2-expressing cells in hand2 mutants.

claim: The lateral venous progenitor cells may emerge from a hand2-expressing lineage.
source: We can envision a model in which the lateral venous progenitor cells emerge from a hand2-expressing lineage, and hand2 influences a cell fate decision between IM and venous identities.
evidence: Speculation about lineage relationships and cell fate decisions.

claim: hand2 normally inhibits IM specification within a portion of the hand2-expressing territory, while also promoting the differentiation of these same hand2-expressing cells into lateral venous progenitors.
source: In particular, we suggest that hand2 normally inhibits IM specification within a portion of the hand2-expressing territory, while also promoting the differentiation of these same hand2-expressing cells into lateral venous progenitors.
evidence: Speculation about the mechanism by which hand2 regulates cell fate decisions.

claim: hand2 could have completely separable effects on the kidney and vein lineages.
source: On the other hand, it remains feasible that hand2 could have completely separable effects on the kidney and vein lineages.
evidence: Speculation about alternative interpretation of hand2 function.

claim: Hand2 could act directly to repress transcription of IM genes.
source: It is plausible that Hand2 could act directly to repress transcription of IM genes, especially considering that ChIP-seq analysis in the mouse limb bud has revealed Hand2-binding peaks associated with Pax2 and Lhx1a (Osterwalder et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on ChIP-seq data from Osterwalder et al., 2014.

claim: Hand2 can influence transcription through DNA-binding-independent mechanisms.
source: Alternatively, Hand2 could repress IM genes without necessarily engaging Hand2-binding sites in their regulatory regions, since Hand2 can influence transcription through DNA-binding-independent mechanisms (Funato et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on prior studies by Funato et al., 2009 and Liu et al., 2009.

claim: Hand2 could regulate IM gene expression indirectly.
source: Of course, Hand2 could also regulate IM gene expression indirectly.
evidence: Speculation about alternative mechanism of Hand2 function.

claim: hand2 overexpression inhibits the expression of vessel progenitor markers in the anterior mesoderm.
source: Along those lines, it is noteworthy that our findings have demonstrated a difference between the functions of hand2 during vessel progenitor development in the anterior and posterior mesoderm: while we have previously shown that hand2 overexpression inhibits the expression of vessel progenitor markers in the anterior mesoderm (Schindler et al., 2014), here we observed expanded expression of the same markers in the posterior mesoderm of hand2-overexpressing embryos.
evidence: Based on prior study by Schindler et al., 2014.

claim: hand2 overexpression expands expression of vessel progenitor markers in the posterior mesoderm.
source: Along those lines, it is noteworthy that our findings have demonstrated a difference between the functions of hand2 during vessel progenitor development in the anterior and posterior mesoderm: while we have previously shown that hand2 overexpression inhibits the expression of vessel progenitor markers in the anterior mesoderm (Schindler et al., 2014), here we observed expanded expression of the same markers in the posterior mesoderm of hand2-overexpressing embryos.
evidence: Based on in situ hybridization data showing expanded etv2 and tal1 expression in the posterior mesoderm following hand2 overexpression.

claim: The distinct responses to hand2 activity in the anterior and posterior mesoderm may reflect regional differences in the utilization of different bHLH binding partners.
source: These distinct responses to hand2 activity in the anterior and posterior mesoderm may reflect regional differences in in the utilization of different bHLH binding partners or in the implementation of the different molecular functions ascribed to Hand2 (Firulli et al., 2005; Funato et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009; McFadden et al., 2002; Schindler et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on prior studies about Hand2 molecular functions.

claim: The distinct responses to hand2 activity in the anterior and posterior mesoderm may reflect regional differences in the implementation of the different molecular functions ascribed to Hand2.
source: These distinct responses to hand2 activity in the anterior and posterior mesoderm may reflect regional differences in in the utilization of different bHLH binding partners or in the implementation of the different molecular functions ascribed to Hand2 (Firulli et al., 2005; Funato et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2009; McFadden et al., 2002; Schindler et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation based on prior studies about Hand2 molecular functions.

claim: osr1 has a non-autonomous role during IM development.
source: It is important to note that prior studies have suggested a non-autonomous role for osr1 during IM development (Mudumana et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on prior study by Mudumana et al., 2008.

claim: hand2 likely affects IM formation from its position in the lateral mesoderm, rather than from the endoderm.
source: In contrast, we suspect that hand2 affects IM formation from its position in the lateral mesoderm, rather than from the endoderm.
evidence: Based on observation of ectopic Pax2a+ cells within hand2-expressing mesoderm and normal endoderm in hans6 mutants.

claim: Alteration of HAND2 function may allow for enhancement of current protocols for generating kidney progenitor cells in vitro.
source: Alteration of HAND2 function may allow for enhancement of current protocols for generating kidney progenitor cells in vitro (Kumar et al., 2015; Mae et al., 2013; Taguchi et al., 2014; Takasato et al., 2014; Takasato et al., 2015), potentially facilitating the requisite control that will be essential for future deployment in patient applications.
evidence: Speculation about potential applications based on current study findings and prior protocols for generating kidney progenitor cells.
